steps.text: Welcome to numerical analysis! Let's start with a small experiment. Type the calculation \(0.1 + 0.2\) into almost any programming language (Python, JavaScript, Swift …). The answer is:
steps.explanation:
And the comparison \(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3\) even returns “false”.

Is the computer broken? No. It calculates with a finite number of digits – and that is exactly where all of numerical analysis begins.

In this lesson you will understand step by step where this tiny deviation comes from, how large such errors can get at most and when they become dangerous.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Does the computer calculate wrongly?
steps.insight: Computers store numbers with a limited number of digits. That is why almost every real number has to be rounded.

steps.text: You already know the problem from your calculator. A calculator with 10 digits computes \(1 : 3\) and shows \(0.3333333333\). If you multiply the result by \(3\) again, you get:
steps.explanation:
What happened?
• \(\frac{1}{3} = 0.3333\ldots\) has infinitely many digits.
• The calculator stores only 10 of them – the rest is cut off.
• This tiny error (\(\approx 3 \cdot 10^{-11}\)) is now part of the result and is carried along by the multiplication with \(3\).

\(0.30000000000000004\) comes about in exactly the same way: the computer cannot even store \(0.1\) exactly. Why \(0.1\) in particular does not fit is explained in Chapter 5.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Does the computer calculate wrongly?
steps.insight: A rounding error occurs when a number needs more digits than there is room for. It is tiny, but it is carried along.

steps.text:
Do such tiny errors matter at all? Usually not – but sometimes a lot.

A well-known example: in the 1991 Gulf War, a missile defence system counted time in steps of \(0.1\) seconds. The number \(0.1\) was stored only approximately, and the error per step was about \(10^{-7}\) seconds.
steps.explanation:
An error of \(10^{-7}\) seconds is ridiculously small. But the system had been running for about \(100\) hours without a restart. During that time \(0.1\) was added \(3.6\) million times, and the errors added up:

\(3.6 \cdot 10^{6} \cdot 10^{-7}\,\text{s} \approx 0.34\,\text{s}\)

In \(0.34\) seconds a fast missile travels more than half a kilometre. The system looked for the target in the wrong place and missed it.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Does the computer calculate wrongly?
steps.insight: Single rounding errors are harmless. It becomes dangerous when many of them add up or when a calculation magnifies them strongly.

steps.text: Numerical analysis is the part of mathematics that develops and studies computational methods for computers. We meet four kinds of errors:
steps.explanation:
• Model errors: the formula describes reality only approximately (e.g. air resistance neglected).
• Data errors: the inputs are measurements and therefore inexact.
• Method (truncation) errors: a method only approximates the exact result (e.g. stopping after 10 steps).
• Rounding errors: the computer calculates with finitely many digits.

This lesson is about rounding errors. Our roadmap:
1. How do we measure errors? (absolute and relative)
2. Floating-point numbers on a simple toy calculator
3. Why \(0.1\) does not fit into the binary system
4. The format IEEE 754 that all computers use
5. What happens during arithmetic – and the dangerous cancellation
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Does the computer calculate wrongly?
steps.insight: Numerical analysis does not only ask “How do I compute this?” but also “How accurate is my result?”.

steps.text:
Before we study errors we need a way to measure them. We call the exact value \(x\) and the approximation (e.g. the stored value) \(\tilde{x}\), read “x tilde”.

The most obvious quantity is the distance between the two:
steps.explanation:
Examples:
• Exact \(x = 2.5\), stored \(\tilde{x} = 2.4\): absolute error \(|2.4 - 2.5| = 0.1\).
• Exact \(x = 1000\), stored \(\tilde{x} = 1003\): absolute error \(3\).

The absolute value makes sure it does not matter whether too much or too little was stored.
steps.insight: The absolute error says by how much you are off – in the same unit as the number itself.

steps.text: Is an absolute error of \(1\) metre a lot or a little? It depends!
steps.explanation:
• You measure the length of a football pitch (\(100\) m) and get \(101\) m. Error: \(1\) m. That is pretty good.
• You measure the length of a table (\(1\) m) and get \(2\) m. Error: also \(1\) m. That is a disaster.

The absolute error is the same in both cases, but the results are completely different in usefulness. What matters is how large the error is compared with the number itself.
steps.insight: An error is only meaningful in relation to the size of the number.

steps.text: That is why we divide the absolute error by the absolute value of the exact value. This gives the relative error:
steps.explanation:
For the two measurements:
• Football pitch: \(\frac{|101 - 100|}{100} = \frac{1}{100} = 0.01 = 1\,\%\)
• Table: \(\frac{|2 - 1|}{1} = 1 = 100\,\%\)

Now you see at once which measurement is useful. The relative error has no unit and is often given in percent.
steps.insight: Relative error = absolute error divided by the size of the number. It has no unit and can be compared.

steps.text: The relative error is closely related to the number of correct (significant) digits. Rule of thumb:
steps.explanation:
Example: \(\pi = 3.14159\ldots\) is approximated by \(3.14\).
• Absolute error: \(|3.14 - 3.14159\ldots| \approx 0.0016\)
• Relative error: \(\frac{0.0016}{3.14159} \approx 5 \cdot 10^{-4}\)

That lies between \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-4}\), and indeed the first 3 digits \(3, 1, 4\) are correct.

Second example: \(\frac{22}{7} = 3.142857\ldots\) has relative error \(\approx 4 \cdot 10^{-4}\) – also about 3 significant digits.
steps.insight: A relative error of about \(10^{-k}\) means roughly \(k\) correct digits – no matter how large the number is.

steps.text: Quick check: a measuring device shows \(\tilde{x} = 0.0011\), the true value is \(x = 0.0010\). Is that accurate? Think for a moment before reading on.
steps.explanation:
• Absolute error: \(|0.0011 - 0.0010| = 0.0001 = 10^{-4}\). That sounds tiny.
• Relative error: \(\frac{10^{-4}}{10^{-3}} = 0.1 = 10\,\%\). That is quite inaccurate!

For very small numbers the absolute error is almost always small – but that says nothing about quality. Only the relative error shows that even the second digit is wrong.
steps.insight: For small numbers the absolute error is misleading. That is why numerical analysis almost always looks at the relative error.

steps.text: How does a computer store numbers that can be very large or very small? With the same idea as scientific notation in physics:
steps.explanation:
You write down only the important digits (\(6.022\) or \(1.6\)) and record in the power of ten where the decimal point actually is.

So the point “floats” to a different position depending on the number – hence the name floating-point number.
steps.insight: Floating-point number = a few digits + a power of ten that fixes the position of the point.

steps.text: So that we can check everything by hand, we build a toy calculator. It stores every number in the form
steps.explanation:
The parts:
• \(d_0.d_1 d_2\) is called the mantissa (or significand). It has exactly \(t = 3\) digits.
• \(e\) is called the exponent. It lies between \(-9\) and \(9\).
• \(10\) is the base.

Examples:
• \(352 = 3.52 \cdot 10^{2}\)
• \(0.0471 = 4.71 \cdot 10^{-2}\)
• \(-7 = -7.00 \cdot 10^{0}\)
steps.insight: Our toy calculator: base 10, mantissa with 3 digits, exponent from −9 to 9. Real computers work exactly the same way – just with base 2 and more digits.

steps.text: Why do we require \(d_0 \neq 0\)? Without this rule the same number could be written in many ways:
steps.explanation:
With only 3 digits, \(0.35 \cdot 10^{3} = 350\) is no longer the same number: the leading zero wasted a digit and the \(2\) got lost.

The rule “the first digit is not zero” is called normalisation. It has two advantages:
• Every number has exactly one representation.
• All 3 digits carry information – no digit is wasted.
steps.insight: Normalised means: the first digit of the mantissa is not zero. That way the precision is fully used.

steps.text: Which numbers can the toy calculator store exactly? Only those that get by with 3 digits. All others have to be rounded.
steps.explanation:
Fits exactly:
• \(250 = 2.50 \cdot 10^{2}\) ✓
• \(0.125\)? These are the digits \(1, 2, 5\): \(1.25 \cdot 10^{-1}\) ✓

Does not fit:
• \(1234\) needs 4 digits ✗
• \(1.005\) needs 4 digits ✗
• \(\frac{1}{3} = 0.333\ldots\) needs infinitely many ✗
• neither does \(\pi\) ✗

The numbers that fit exactly are called machine numbers. There are only finitely many of them.
steps.insight: Machine numbers are the numbers the computer can represent exactly. All other real numbers are rounded to a machine number.

steps.text: Rounding goes to the nearest machine number. We write \(\operatorname{fl}(x)\) (“float of x”):
steps.explanation:
How to proceed:
1. Write the number normalised: \(1234 = 1.234 \cdot 10^{3}\).
2. Round after the third digit: \(1.234 \to 1.23\).

For \(\frac{2}{3} = 6.666\ldots \cdot 10^{-1}\) we round up: \(6.67 \cdot 10^{-1}\).

If a number lies exactly halfway (e.g. \(2.345\)), computers round to the even last digit, i.e. \(2.34\). This prevents errors from always going in the same direction. For our calculations this special case hardly matters.
steps.insight: \(\operatorname{fl}(x)\) is the machine number closest to \(x\).

steps.text: How large is the rounding error? Let's work out two examples:
steps.explanation:
The absolute errors are completely different: \(4\) versus \(0.000045\) – a factor of \(100\,000\).

The relative errors, however, are almost the same, both about \(3 \cdot 10^{-3}\).

This is no coincidence: whether the number is large or small is handled only by the exponent. The mantissa always has 3 digits, so the relative accuracy is always about the same.
steps.insight: Floating-point numbers have (almost) constant relative error. That is exactly why numerical analysis measures relatively.

steps.text: How large can the relative rounding error get at most? When rounding to 3 digits, the error is at most half a unit of the last digit.
steps.explanation:
Why exactly this number? Look at numbers with mantissa between \(1.00\) and \(9.99\):
• The last digit has the value \(0.01\), so the rounding error is at most \(0.005\).
• Relatively, it is worst when the mantissa is as small as possible, i.e. close to \(1.00\).

Example: \(1.005\) lies exactly between \(1.00\) and \(1.01\). Error \(0.005\), relative \(\frac{0.005}{1.005} \approx 5 \cdot 10^{-3}\).

For a mantissa close to \(9.99\), on the other hand, the relative error is only about \(\frac{0.005}{9.99} \approx 5 \cdot 10^{-4}\).

The bound \(u\) is called the unit roundoff.
steps.insight: For every number in the representable range: relative rounding error \(\le u\). In the toy calculator \(u = 0.005\).

steps.text: The bound can also be written as an equation. This is the form numerical analysts calculate with:
steps.explanation:
\(\delta\) is simply the relative error with its sign:
\(\delta = \frac{\operatorname{fl}(x) - x}{x}\).

Example: \(x = 1234\), \(\operatorname{fl}(x) = 1230\):
\(\delta = \frac{1230 - 1234}{1234} \approx -0.0032\), and indeed \(|\delta| \le 0.005\).

This notation is handy because you can keep calculating with \((1 + \delta)\) like with a small perturbation factor.
steps.insight: Rounding means: multiply the number by a factor \((1 + \delta)\) with \(|\delta| \le u\).

steps.text: The toy calculator has a second limit: the exponent. It only runs from \(-9\) to \(9\).
steps.explanation:
What happens outside?
• Overflow: \(5.00 \cdot 10^{6} \cdot 3.00 \cdot 10^{5} = 1.5 \cdot 10^{12}\). That is too large. Real computers then return “infinity”.
• Underflow: \(1.00 \cdot 10^{-5} \cdot 1.00 \cdot 10^{-6} = 10^{-11}\). That is too small and becomes \(0\).

Underflow sounds harmless but can be treacherous: if you later divide by this result, you divide by \(0\).
steps.insight: Floating-point numbers have two limits: limited precision (mantissa) and limited range (exponent).

steps.text: How are the machine numbers spread along the number line? Let's count the toy calculator's numbers between \(1\) and \(10\):
steps.explanation:
These are \(900\) numbers with spacing \(0.01\).

Between \(10\) and \(100\): \(1.00 \cdot 10^{1}, 1.01 \cdot 10^{1}, \ldots\), i.e. \(10.0, 10.1, 10.2, \ldots, 99.9\) – again \(900\) numbers, but now with spacing \(0.1\).

Between \(100\) and \(1000\): \(100, 101, \ldots, 999\) – spacing \(1\).

So every decade contains the same number of machine numbers. The larger the range, the larger the gaps.
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The gaps between the numbers
steps.insight: Machine numbers are not evenly spread: with every power of ten the gaps become ten times larger.

steps.text: With real computers (base \(2\)) it is the same, except that the gaps double at every power of two. The animation shows a tiny binary system with 3 mantissa digits.
steps.explanation:
Watch:
• \([1, 2)\) contains 4 machine numbers with spacing \(0.25\).
• \([2, 4)\) again contains 4 numbers, but with spacing \(0.5\).
• \([4, 8)\) again 4 numbers with spacing \(1\).

The gap grows with the number – but relative to the number it stays about the same size.
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The gaps between the numbers
steps.insight: Absolute gaps grow, relative gaps stay the same. That is the basic idea of every floating-point representation.

steps.text: One gap is especially important: the one right after \(1\). In the toy calculator the next number after \(1.00\) is \(1.01\). This distance is called machine epsilon:
steps.explanation:
In general, for base \(b\) and \(t\) mantissa digits: \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} = b^{1-t}\).

The unit roundoff \(u\) is exactly half of it: whoever rounds to the nearest machine number is off by at most half a gap.

Beware of a common mix-up: \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}\) is NOT the smallest positive number. The smallest positive number is \(10^{-9}\) – much smaller. \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}\) describes the precision, not the range.
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The gaps between the numbers
steps.insight: \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}\) is the distance from \(1\) to the next larger machine number. It measures the relative precision of the computer.

steps.text: A surprising consequence: in the toy calculator
steps.explanation:
The number \(1.004\) is closer to \(1.00\) than to \(1.01\) and is therefore rounded to \(1.00\). Adding \(0.004\) does nothing at all!

With \(0.006\) it is different: \(1.006\) is rounded to \(1.01\).

Rule of thumb: if something smaller than \(u\) is added to \(1\), nothing changes. Real computers show the same: there \(1 + 10^{-16} = 1\).
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The gaps between the numbers
steps.insight: For \(|x| < u\) the computer gives \(1 + x = 1\). Summands that are too small are “swallowed”.

steps.text: Real computers do not calculate in base \(10\) but in base \(2\). A short review of the binary system: the digits have the values \(\ldots, 4, 2, 1\) before the point and \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{8}, \ldots\) after the point.
steps.explanation:
Two more examples:
• \((0.11)_2 = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} = 0.75\)
• \((10.01)_2 = 2 + \frac{1}{4} = 2.25\)

The small subscript \(2\) indicates that the number is written in binary.
steps.section: Chapter 5 · The computer works in binary
steps.insight: In binary, the digits after the point stand for halves, quarters, eighths, sixteenths …

steps.text: How do you write a decimal number like \(0.375\) in binary? With a simple trick: keep doubling. The part before the point is always the next binary digit.
steps.explanation:
Result: \(0.375 = (0.011)_2\).

Check: \(\frac{0}{2} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{8} = 0.25 + 0.125 = 0.375\) ✓

Why does this work? In binary, doubling shifts the point one place to the right. The digit that slides in front of the point is exactly the next digit after the point.
steps.section: Chapter 5 · The computer works in binary
steps.insight: Decimal → binary (fractional part): double, write down the digit before the point, continue with the rest.

steps.text: Now the puzzle from the beginning. We convert \(0.1\):
steps.explanation:
From here on everything repeats: \(0.2 \to 0.4 \to 0.8 \to 0.6 \to 0.2 \to \ldots\)

So
\(0.1 = (0.0\,0011\,0011\,0011\ldots)_2\)

The digit block \(0011\) repeats forever. But a computer has only finitely many digits and must cut off and round somewhere. That is why \(0.1\) inside the computer is not exactly \(0.1\).
steps.section: Chapter 5 · The computer works in binary
steps.insight: \(0.1\) has infinitely many digits in binary – just like \(\frac{1}{3}\) in decimal.

steps.text:
Quick check: which of these numbers can a computer store exactly?
\(0.5\), \(0.25\), \(0.2\), \(0.75\), \(0.3\)
steps.explanation:
Exactly storable are \(0.5 = \frac{1}{2}\), \(0.25 = \frac{1}{4}\) and \(0.75 = \frac{3}{4}\).

Not exact are \(0.2 = \frac{1}{5}\) and \(0.3 = \frac{3}{10}\).

The rule behind it: a (reduced) fraction has a finite binary representation exactly when its denominator is a power of two. The denominator of \(\frac{1}{10}\) contains the factor \(5\) – that does not fit.

For comparison in decimal: there, fractions whose denominators consist of twos and fives are finite (\(\frac{1}{4} = 0.25\)), but \(\frac{1}{3}\) is not.
steps.section: Chapter 5 · The computer works in binary
steps.insight: Finite in binary ⇔ the reduced denominator is a power of two. Most “round” decimal numbers are infinitely long in binary.

steps.text: Now we can fully explain \(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004\). Three roundings take place:
steps.explanation:
1. \(0.1\) is stored – slightly too large.
2. \(0.2\) is stored – also slightly too large.
3. The sum is rounded and lands on the machine number just above \(0.3\).

The number \(0.3\) itself, however, is rounded to the machine number just below \(0.3\). The two results are neighbouring machine numbers, but not the same one. That is why the comparison “equal?” is false, and printing 17 digits reveals the \(4\) at the end.
steps.section: Chapter 5 · The computer works in binary
steps.insight: The deviation does not come from an arithmetic mistake but from the fact that the inputs were already rounded.

steps.text: This leads to an important rule for every program: never test floating-point numbers for exact equality. Instead, ask whether they are close enough.
steps.explanation:
With a relative tolerance such as \(\text{tol} = 10^{-12}\) we then get \(0.1 + 0.2 \approx 0.3\) ✓.

Another example of the same problem: adding \(0.1\) ten times gives \(0.9999999999999999\) on a computer instead of \(1\). A loop “while \(x \neq 1\)” would never end!
steps.section: Chapter 5 · The computer works in binary
steps.insight: Floating-point numbers are compared with a tolerance, not with “==”.

steps.text: Almost all computers use the format IEEE 754. The most important variant is called double precision. A number occupies \(64\) bits there, split into three parts:
steps.explanation:
• 1 sign bit \(s\): \(0\) for plus, \(1\) for minus.
• 11 bits for the exponent \(E\).
• 52 bits for the mantissa \(f\) (the digits after the point).

This is exactly our toy calculator – just with base \(2\), many more mantissa digits and a much larger exponent range.
steps.insight: double = 1 sign bit + 11 exponent bits + 52 mantissa bits = 64 bits.

steps.text: The value of a double number is computed like this:
steps.explanation:
Two tricks are hidden in it:
• Hidden bit: a normalised binary number always starts with \(1\). This \(1\) does not need to be stored! So the mantissa effectively has \(53\) digits although only \(52\) are stored.
• Bias of \(1023\): the stored exponent \(E\) is always positive. Subtracting \(1023\) also gives negative exponents.

Example \(1.0\): \(s = 0\), \(E = 1023\), \(f = 0\), because \(1.0 = (1.0)_2 \cdot 2^{0}\).
steps.insight: The leading 1 is not stored (hidden bit). The exponent is stored with a bias of 1023.

steps.text: A complete example: how is \(-6.5\) stored?
steps.explanation:
Read off:
• Sign: negative, so \(s = 1\).
• Exponent: \(2\), stored as \(E = 2 + 1023 = 1025\).
• Mantissa: after the hidden \(1\) come the digits \(101\), then only zeros: \(f = 1010000\ldots0\).

Check: \((-1)^{1} \cdot (1.101)_2 \cdot 2^{1025 - 1023} = -(1 + 0.5 + 0.125) \cdot 4 = -1.625 \cdot 4 = -6.5\) ✓
steps.insight: Procedure: write the number in binary, normalise to \(1.\ldots \cdot 2^{e}\), then read off sign, \(E = e + 1023\) and mantissa.

steps.text: What do the 53 mantissa digits mean for precision? As in the toy calculator, \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} = b^{1-t}\), now with \(b = 2\) and \(t = 53\):
steps.explanation:
In plain words: every number is stored with a relative error of at most about \(10^{-16}\). That is roughly 16 significant decimal digits.

The 11-bit exponent allows a huge range:
• largest number \(\approx 1.8 \cdot 10^{308}\)
• smallest normalised positive number \(\approx 2.2 \cdot 10^{-308}\)

For comparison: the entire observable universe contains only about \(10^{80}\) atoms.
steps.insight: double: about 16 significant decimal digits, numbers up to about \(10^{308}\).

steps.text: Besides double there is the smaller format single precision (“float” in many languages). A comparison:
steps.explanation:
single needs only half the memory and is faster on graphics cards. In return you only get about 7 significant digits.

The missile example from Chapter 1 shows why that can be critical: whoever sums up for a long time quickly loses accuracy with few digits.

Scientific computing therefore almost always uses double. From now on, “floating-point number” means double.
steps.insight: single: ≈ 7 digits, double: ≈ 16 digits. The standard in numerical analysis is double.

steps.text: IEEE 754 also specifies what happens in special cases instead of letting the program crash:
steps.explanation:
• \(\pm\infty\) (Inf): on overflow or for \(1 / 0\). You can keep calculating: \(\infty + 1 = \infty\).
• NaN (“Not a Number”): for undefined expressions such as \(0 / 0\), \(\infty - \infty\) or \(\sqrt{-1}\). Every calculation involving NaN gives NaN again.
• Subnormal numbers: between \(0\) and the smallest normalised number there are some further numbers with a leading \(0\). This makes the transition to zero smoother.

Practical tip: if NaN shows up in a result, a forbidden operation happened somewhere before – often a division by a number that became \(0\) through underflow.
steps.insight: Inf and NaN are not a crash but a warning sign: somewhere an overflow or an undefined operation occurred.

steps.text: What happens when the computer combines two machine numbers? IEEE 754 guarantees: the result is as if the computation had been done exactly and then rounded once.
steps.explanation:
Example in the toy calculator (\(u = 0.005\)):
\(1.23 \cdot 4.56 = 5.6088\) exactly, stored is \(5.61\).

Relative error: \(\frac{5.61 - 5.6088}{5.6088} \approx 2.1 \cdot 10^{-4} \le 0.005\) ✓

So every single arithmetic operation is as accurate as it can possibly be. Problems only arise when many operations are chained together.
steps.insight: Each single basic operation on a computer has relative error at most \(u\).

steps.text: Something special happens in addition: before adding, both numbers must have the same exponent. For that, the smaller number is shifted to the right.
steps.explanation:
When the exponents are aligned, the \(4\) slides into the fourth place after the point – and there is no room there. After rounding it is gone:
\(\operatorname{fl}(1000 + 4) = 1000\).

This is the same phenomenon as \(1 + 0.004 = 1\) from Chapter 4, just for larger numbers.
steps.insight: If one summand is much smaller than the other, it is cut off completely or partly when the exponents are aligned.

steps.text: One consequence: the order of addition matters! Compute \(1000 + 4 + 4\) in the toy calculator in two ways:
steps.explanation:
First order: the \(4\) is swallowed twice, one at a time. Result \(1000\), error \(8\).

Second order: the small numbers are added first. \(8\) is large enough to count: \(1008\) is rounded to \(1.01 \cdot 10^{3} = 1010\). Error only \(2\).

So the associative law \((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\) no longer holds exactly on a computer!
steps.insight: Floating-point addition is not associative. The result can depend on the order.

steps.text: An even clearer example. The toy calculator is to compute the sum \(1 + \underbrace{0.001 + 0.001 + \ldots + 0.001}_{1000\text{ times}}\). Exactly, that is \(2\).
steps.explanation:
Variant A, from left to right:
\(1 + 0.001 = 1.001 \to 1.00\). Every single summand is swallowed. After 1000 additions the result is still \(1.00\). Error: \(100\,\%\) of the increase!

Variant B, small numbers first:
\(0.001 + 0.001 = 0.002\), then \(0.003\), …, \(0.999\), \(1.00\). All these partial sums fit exactly into 3 digits. Finally \(1.00 + 1 = 2.00\) ✓

The same numbers, the same operations – only the order is different.
steps.insight: Rule of thumb: add many numbers from the smallest to the largest.

steps.text:
Quick check: which arithmetic laws still hold exactly on a computer?
• \(a + b = b + a\)
• \(a \cdot b = b \cdot a\)
• \((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\)
• \(a \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot c\)
steps.explanation:
The commutative laws still hold: \(a + b\) and \(b + a\) give exactly the same result, because they are equal when computed exactly and are rounded the same way.

The associative and distributive laws, however, no longer hold: the two sides are rounded a different number of times and at different places.

That is why the same program with rearranged formulas can produce slightly different numbers.
steps.insight: Commutative: yes. Associative and distributive: no. Mathematically equal formulas can give different results on a computer.

steps.text:
Now comes the most dangerous effect of floating-point arithmetic: cancellation. It occurs when two numbers of almost the same size are subtracted.

An example in the toy calculator: let the exact values be \(a = 1.234\) and \(b = 1.226\). We want \(a - b\).
steps.explanation:
Both numbers are rounded to \(1.23\). The difference was hidden precisely in the fourth digit – and the computer does not have it.

The result \(0\) has a relative error of \(100\,\%\), although both inputs were stored with an error of only \(0.3\,\%\).
steps.insight: Cancellation: in the difference of nearly equal numbers, tiny relative errors can turn into huge ones.

steps.text: Why does this happen? The animation shows two numbers with 6 significant digits each, whose last digit is slightly uncertain.
steps.explanation:
The leading digits \(1.2345\) agree and cancel in the subtraction. Only the trailing digits remain – and those were exactly the uncertain ones.

Important: the subtraction itself is exact! It creates no new error. It only makes the old error visible because the result is so small: a small absolute error becomes a large relative error for a small number (compare the quick check in Chapter 2).
steps.insight: Cancellation does not create an error – it magnifies the error that is already in the inputs.

steps.text: A classic example is the formula for quadratic equations. Consider
steps.explanation:
The square root \(\sqrt{10^{16} - 4}\) is almost exactly \(10^{8}\).

• Large root (with \(+\)): \(x_1 = \frac{10^8 + 10^8}{2} \approx 10^{8}\). Here we add – no problem.
• Small root (with \(-\)): the square root is about \(10^{8} - 2 \cdot 10^{-8}\). So the numerator is \(10^{8} - (10^{8} - 2 \cdot 10^{-8})\) – a difference of nearly equal numbers: cancellation!

A computer with double returns for the small root:
\(x_2 \approx 7.45 \cdot 10^{-9}\)

The correct value is \(x_2 \approx 1.00 \cdot 10^{-8}\). The result is off by about \(25\,\%\) – despite 16 digits of precision!
steps.insight: The well-known quadratic formula is prone to cancellation for one of the two roots when \(b^2\) is much larger than \(4ac\).

steps.text: The fix: avoid the subtraction. By Vieta's formula, \(x_1 \cdot x_2 = q\) always holds for \(x^2 + px + q = 0\).
steps.explanation:
The stable procedure:
1. Compute the root of larger magnitude with the formula – there we add, not subtract.
2. Get the smaller root via Vieta: \(x_2 = \frac{q}{x_1}\). A division is harmless.

Mathematically both ways are equivalent. Numerically the second one is much better.

This is a core idea of numerical analysis: formulas that are equal on paper can behave very differently on a computer.
steps.insight: Rewriting helps against cancellation: the dangerous difference is replaced by a harmless calculation.

steps.text: Second example: \(\sqrt{x + 1} - \sqrt{x}\) for large \(x\), say \(x = 10^{12}\). Both roots are almost equal – cancellation threatens. The trick: expand with the difference-of-squares formula.
steps.explanation:
The numerator becomes \((x + 1) - x = 1\). The difference has disappeared; we only add and divide.

Results with double for \(x = 10^{12}\):
• directly: \(5.000038 \cdot 10^{-7}\) – only about 5 digits correct
• rewritten: \(4.999999999999 \cdot 10^{-7}\) – practically all digits correct

The direct way loses about 11 of the 16 digits.
steps.insight: Differences of square roots are defused by multiplying with the sum (difference of squares).

steps.text: Third example: \(1 - \cos x\) for small \(x\). Since \(\cos x\) is almost \(1\) for small \(x\), the difference cancels. A trigonometric identity helps here:
steps.explanation:
For \(x = 10^{-8}\) the computer returns:
• directly: \(\cos(10^{-8})\) is rounded to exactly \(1\), so \(1 - \cos x = 0\). Completely wrong!
• rewritten: \(2 \sin^2(0.5 \cdot 10^{-8}) = 5.0 \cdot 10^{-17}\) ✓

Check with the Taylor series: \(1 - \cos x \approx \frac{x^2}{2} = \frac{10^{-16}}{2} = 5 \cdot 10^{-17}\) ✓
steps.insight: If a formula cancels for small (or large) values, look for an equivalent formula without the difference – often using identities or Taylor series.

steps.text:
Quick check: for which calculations is there a risk of cancellation if \(a\) and \(b\) are positive and \(a \approx b\)?
• \(a + b\)
• \(a - b\)
• \(a \cdot b\)
• \(a : b\)
steps.explanation:
Only for \(a - b\).

• \(a + b\) with equal signs: the relative errors average out, nothing is magnified.
• \(a \cdot b\) and \(a : b\): the relative errors merely add – \(10^{-16}\) becomes at most about \(2 \cdot 10^{-16}\).
• \(a - b\) with \(a \approx b\): the result is much smaller than the inputs, the relative error is magnified by the factor \(\frac{|a|}{|a - b|}\).

Beware: \(a + b\) with different signs is really a subtraction and just as vulnerable.
steps.insight: Only subtracting numbers of almost equal size is dangerous. Multiplying, dividing and adding numbers of equal sign are harmless.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Measuring errors: absolute \(|\tilde{x} - x|\), relative \(\frac{|\tilde{x} - x|}{|x|}\). Relative error \(10^{-k}\) ≈ \(k\) significant digits.

2. Floating-point numbers: \(\pm\,\text{mantissa} \cdot b^{e}\), normalised. There are only finitely many machine numbers, and the gaps grow with the number.

3. Rounding: \(\operatorname{fl}(x) = x(1 + \delta)\) with \(|\delta| \le u\). Machine epsilon \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} = b^{1-t}\), \(u = \varepsilon_{\text{mach}} / 2\).

4. Binary: \(0.1\) is infinitely long, hence \(0.1 + 0.2 \neq 0.3\). Always compare with a tolerance.

5. IEEE 754 double: 64 bits, \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} = 2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \cdot 10^{-16}\), about 16 digits.

6. Arithmetic: each operation has error \(\le u\), but addition is not associative – small summands first.

7. Cancellation in \(a - b\) with \(a \approx b\): avoid it by rewriting (Vieta, difference of squares, identities).
steps.insight: Key message of the lesson: the computer performs each single operation almost perfectly – but clumsy formulas can make small errors huge.

steps.text: What comes next? In this lesson you saw that some calculations strongly magnify small errors. In the next lesson “Conditioning & Stability” we turn this into a precise tool:
steps.explanation:
• The condition number measures how strongly a problem magnifies input errors – regardless of how you compute it.
• Stability judges whether a computational method does additional damage – like the naive quadratic formula.

With this you will be able to explain, for example, why the quadratic formula is unstable while the problem itself is harmless.
steps.insight: Next step: clearly distinguish conditioning (problem) and stability (method).
